felix-o-day:
F. Hopkinson Smith's Felix O'Day opens on Broadway in the rain, the Great White Way splashed with liquid jewels. Playhouses blaze, crowds surge, and street urchins clutch gallery money. Against this glitter the novel sets its hero, glimpsed some ten years before the main action. Felix O'Day is an Irish gentleman ruined and exiled by a family disgrace.

In New York he works humbly in an antique shop, hiding his name and his past. A stolen miniature, a young girl's ruin, and his own wife's betrayal knot the plot. Smith, engineer, painter, and raconteur, loved the city's clerks and curio dealers. His Felix keeps a gentleman's honour in a shopkeeper's apron. The novel is his most popular fiction, a romance of redemption among Broadway's lights, where the moth found in the mud at dawn is answered by one man's quiet restitution.
five-little-peppers-midway:
Five Little Peppers Midway continues the Pepper family stories by Margaret Sidney, who dedicates the book to her own little Margaret, known to readers as Phronsie. Sidney returns to the little brown house and its five children, now older, busier, and pulled toward new houses and new duties. The contents open with Phronsie's pie and a visit from Cousin Eunice Chatterton.

Chapter titles map the family's season of change. A rehearsal and a play bring Badgertown callers, then a sudden blow separates the party. Polly takes up new work, news arrives, and Mamsie's wedding crowns the middle of the book. Phronsie vanishes and is found, in the best Pepper tradition of alarm ending in relief. The girls get Polly back for the close. Work, marriage, and sibling loyalty carry these domestic chapters.
foul-play:
Charles Reade and Dion Boucicault joined forces on Foul Play, a sensation novel that opens in a London merchant's dining room. Merchant Wardlaw rules his Russell Square house with iron routine and full dress at dinner. His son Arthur, clerk turned Oxford student, seems set to inherit firm and habits. Tutor Robert Penfold, who owes the family gratitude, guards the young man's studies.

Forgery and a lost ship drive the plot once the opening breaks. Helen Rolleston, a general's daughter, draws the loves of men whose secrets tie back to the Wardlaw firm. James Seaton, a broken man hiding from his past, watches her from the garden shadows. False charges, an insurance mystery, and a hunt for the forger keep the pace. Reade's research habits show in legal and shipping detail. Readers who like sensation fiction, with crime, courtship, and ruined names at stake, get a plate here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BeckRay_Beck_Ra:
More than three years after the assassination, the FBI's Dallas office still carried an open subject line: Assassination of President John F. Kennedy. This memorandum, dated February 23, 1967, went to SAC Gordon Shanklin, the special agent in charge at Dallas, under file 89-43.

The sender's name is garbled in the scan, a reminder of the condition of much of the released paper. Dallas was where the crime happened, and its office held the local file that every new lead, letter, and claim still entered. The single memo is preserved as a page of that file's long afterlife.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BertrandClayDoc:
Clay Bertrand was the name Jim Garrison's investigation chased through New Orleans: the alleged alias of Clay Shaw, the businessman Garrison put on trial for conspiring to kill President Kennedy. These research notes, dated November 23, 1971, come from a researcher's work on that matter after the trial had ended.

The notes record that Ed Planer confirmed Jesse Core appeared in preserved Johann Rush footage, film connected with Dealey Plaza on the day of the assassination. They also record meetings with Garrison himself. Research notes like these are the workshop floor of assassination scholarship: half-checked leads, names, and film references kept for later use.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarcusRay_Marcu:
Raymond Marcus published 'Truth vs. Political Truth' as a collection of essays, and this is volume one, dated August 2001. Marcus writes about media elites and how they shape public opinion. His central subject is the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the way it has been covered.

Marcus was a longtime researcher who argued that the press protected the official account. The essays measure news coverage against the evidence as he read it. For readers, the volume offers one researcher's case that political convenience, not proof, settled the story in print. It appeared nearly forty years after Dallas, in a debate that had by then moved from commissions to talk shows and the early internet.
gower-latin-works-macaulay:
George Macaulay's Complete Works of John Gower gathered the poet's writings in four volumes at the turn of the century. Volume Three, from 1902, prints Gower's Latin works with notes. Gower wrote in three tongues, and Latin was his language of public warning.

The chief work here is the Vox Clamantis, the Voice of One Crying, on the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the sins of every rank. The Cronica Tripertita treats the fall of Richard II. Shorter Latin poems fill out the volume. Macaulay's editing let English readers meet the stern moralist behind the gentle love poet of the Confessio.
heimskringla-or-the-chronicle-of-the-kin:
Snorri Sturluson, the Icelandic poet and historian, wrote Heimskringla around 1225, a cycle of sagas covering Norway's kings from about 850 to 1177. This English text opens with the sagas of Halfdan the Black and Harald Fairhair, then Hakon the Good and Olaf Trygvason. Snorri worked from skaldic verse, the praise poems he quotes as evidence.

The long middle reaches the saga of Saint Olaf, the largest in the book, and continues through Magnus the Good, Harald Hardrade, and later kings. Battles, sea voyages, and councils fill the pages, told in Snorri's terse, ironic style. Heimskringla remains the chief narrative source for early Norwegian history and a summit of medieval Icelandic prose.
how-to-live-on-24-hours-a-day:
Arnold Bennett addressed the office worker's secret poverty in How to Live on 24 Hours a Day: not money, but time. Bennett argues that the day holds a daily miracle of unspent hours outside work, and that most men fritter them as careless spenders fritter income. His program asks for a modest start: an hour or so of serious reading, reflection, and interest in the arts, protected like a budget.

Chapters cover controlling the mind, the reflective mood, and dangers to avoid, all in Bennett's brisk, funny, elder-brother voice. He scolds, encourages, and sets homework. The little book became the classic of self-improvement literature, and its central claim still stings: you already have the time; you are spending it on nothing.
i-will-repay:
Baroness Orczy's I Will Repay continues the world of the Scarlet Pimpernel in revolutionary Paris. A prologue in 1783 shows a card-table quarrel over the notorious Adèle de Montchéri. The young Vicomte de Marny hurls insults and cards at Paul Déroulède, the rich newcomer. A duel follows, and the boy falls.

De Marny's sister Anne Marie nurses the family's vow: I will repay. Ten years later the Revolution gives her the weapon she needs. Déroulède, now a popular deputy, shelters a persecuted girl in his house. Anne Marie enters his service to destroy him, and loves him instead. Orczy weaves denunciation, prison, and rescue into her melodrama. The Pimpernel himself moves at the edges. Honour and revenge fight for one woman's soul across the Terror.
if-i-may:
A. A. Milne's If I May gathers essays reprinted from The Sphere, The Outlook, The Daily News, The Sunday Express and Vanity Fair, with alterations and additions. Milne, already known for Not That It Matters, writes here before his fame as the creator of Winnie-the-Pooh.

Contents include The Case for the Artist, A London Garden, The Game of Kings, Fixtures and Fittings, Experts, The Robinson Tradition, Getting Things Done, and Christmas Games. Later essays treat the mathematical mind, going out to dinner, the etiquette of escape, and children's plays. Readers who enjoy light, witty essays will find Milne at his most companionable.
ivanoff-a-play:
Anton Chekhov's Ivanoff appears here in an early English translation credited to Anton Checkov. Its cast list is precise. Nicholas Ivanoff serves on the Council of Peasant Affairs. His wife Anna, born Sarah Abramson, is dying of consumption. His uncle Count Shabelski and the Lebedieffs complete the household, and Sasha Lebedieff loves him. Dr Lvoff, young and righteous, watches Ivanoff's debts and depression with disgust.

The stage fills with knick-knacks, revolvers, vodka, and salted herrings as Ivanoff's estate and marriage collapse together. Borkin, his manager, schemes while Sasha offers rescue through love. Chekhov's first full-length play already shows his method: no villains, much talk, and a gun that finally speaks. Its ending still divides audiences between pity and judgment.
keeping-fit-all-the-way:
Keeping Fit All the Way is Walter Camp's book on how to obtain and maintain health, strength, and efficiency. Camp, the famous Yale football coach, wrote it for general readers in 1919. A front photograph shows Camp himself beside ex-President Taft and Colonel Ullman. The three are named pioneers of senior service, the book's program for older men.

Part Two presents the Daily Dozen, Camp's short set of daily exercises. The exercises were devised for busy men who had no time for long training. Camp argues that fitness is a duty, not a hobby, in work and war alike. The book closes with the American Citizen's Creed. It remains the classic statement of Camp's daily-dozen plan.
laugh-and-play:
E. Stuart Hardy made Laugh and Play as a book of original stories for children. Ernest Nister published it in London, with Dutton in New York. Hardy also drew its many pictures.

An opening verse urges children to laugh and play all day. Tears and sighs, it says, make the sky grey. The stories follow that bright advice in tone. Pictures and tales work together on each page. The book was printed in Bavaria, as many fine color books then were. Short, cheerful pieces suit reading aloud to young children. Hardy's pictures give each small tale a friendly face.
little-bear-at-work-and-at-play:
Frances Margaret Fox continues her Little Bear stories here. Warner Carr illustrated this volume of animal tales. Fox dedicates it to girls of Martha Cook Dormitory, Ann Arbor. They earned the honor by loving Little Bear, she writes.

Stories show Little Bear bragging, refusing work, and learning to swim. Mother Skunk helps him in one early adventure. A lost otter baby and a school visit vary the fun. Three bears come to breakfast before his surprise party closes it. Little Bear's promise and three visiting bears fill later chapters. When Mother Skunk helped him opens the animal lessons.
little-folks-astray:
Sophie May published this children's book in 1872. She addresses parents directly before the story begins. The Parlin and Clifford children return from earlier books here. They refused to stay asleep and came downstairs again, she jokes.

Fly Clifford expects to stand in the middle of everything. Grandma Read will talk her down with Quaker speech. Aunt Madge adds a story from her own childhood summer. Lessons on self-will and respect await the little listeners. A fly in a cup of milk pictures overwhelmed Fly Clifford. Elders will have their voice in this volume, May promises.
little-miss-by-the-day:
Lucille Van Slyke published this elusive heroine's story in 1919. A colored frontispiece by Mabel Hatt illustrates the volume. The prologue argues fascinating people often slip away unmet. They leave rooms or towns just before we arrive, she writes.

Miss By-the-Day was just a little seamstress at first hearing. Her odd, drawling way of speaking charmed everyone who repeated it. People smiled dreamily whenever they mentioned her name. Van Slyke had earlier written Eve's Other Children. Geordie receives the book's dedication from Van Slyke. Eve's Other Children preceded this portrait of the seamstress.
man-in-the-iron-mask-an-essay:
The Man in the Iron Mask, an essay by Alexandre Dumas, comes from his Celebrated Crimes. This set of eight volumes was issued in 1910. Dumas warns readers that this is the essay, not his famous novel. For nearly a hundred years, he says, the problem has teased writers.

Who was the masked prisoner of the Bastille, held under strange precautions? No subject, Dumas finds, is more obscure or more attractive. Pity deepens into terror as he dwells on that long captivity. He weighs the theories that historians and romancers have offered. His own elegant answer caps the argument. It is history's classic cold case, told by a master storyteller.
margret-howth-a-story-of-to-day:
Margret Howth, A Story of To-Day, is a novel by Rebecca Harding Davis. The narrator promises a story very homely and narrow in scope. She writes, she says, from the border of the battlefield. A shadow of death has fallen on the land as she begins.

Men have forgotten to hope and forgotten to pray, she writes. Against that gloom she sets the lives of mill-town workers. Margret herself is a young woman of conscience and quiet strength. Davis had already shocked readers with her tale of mill life. Here she joins factory labor to love and moral choice. The novel is a pioneer work of American realism.
martha-by-the-day:
Julie M. Lippmann published Martha By-the-Day in 1912. Her novel opens in New York on a wet November night. Young Claire Lang stands lost in the Broadway rush.

A strong woman seizes Claire and pulls her clear of the traffic. Claire takes the grip for an insult and starts a proud speech. Then she sees her rescuer is a woman, and the scene turns to comedy and the start of a bond. Martha, the day worker of the title, stands behind that rescue. Her size, strength, and plain speech set her apart from Claire's sheltered kin.
mildred-s-inheritance-just-her-way-ann-s:
Annie Fellows Johnston gathers three stories for young readers in this volume of the Cosey Corner Series. The tales are Mildred's Inheritance, Just Her Way, and Ann's Own Way. Johnston was already known for her Little Colonel books, advertised in these pages. Each title names a girl and the test she faces.

An inheritance, a stubborn streak, and a wish to go one's own way drive the three plots. Johnston wrote for girls who liked stories of home, friendship, and character. The publisher priced her books for wide family reading. The volume shows the gentle moral storytelling that made her a favorite children's author.
musicians-of-to-day:
Romain Rolland, famed for Jean-Christophe, wrote these essays on living musicians. Mary Blaiklock translated the book, issued in New York in 1915. Claude Landi added an introduction. Berlioz stands first in the contents.

Wagner gets two parts, on Siegfried and on Tristan. Saint-Saens, Vincent d'Indy, Richard Strauss, and Hugo Wolf follow. Don Lorenzo Perosi represents sacred music in Italy. A closing part weighs French music against German. Rolland writes as a novelist who loved music deeply. His portraits mix praise, doubt, and strong personal taste in a clear, warm style.
myth-and-science-an-essay:
Tito Vignoli's essay appeared in the International Scientific Series in 1885. Kegan Paul issued this third edition in London. Chapter one asks what ideas and sources make myth. Animal sensation and perception come next.

Human sensation follows, then a clear statement of the problem. Vignoli studies how mind works on what the senses give. He traces one law through myth's long growth into science. Dreams, illusions, and madness close the argument. The book treats myth not as error but as mind's first draft. It is a bold early try at a science of how humans explain the world.
nasa-tm-19650010115-inverse-compton-scat:
Frank C Jones at Goddard Space Flight Center is named on the cover of this October 1964 paper, though the scan renders his name poorly. His subject is inverse Compton scattering by cosmic ray electrons. In that process, a fast electron gives energy to a low-energy photon and boosts it to much higher energy.

Jones treats the process as a theory problem in space physics. Cosmic ray electrons move through weak light fields in space, including sunlight. Working out how much light they boost helps explain high-energy radiation seen from space. The paper gives that calculation a careful treatment.
nasa-tm-19660007950-a-digitized-spark-ch:
Charles H Ehrmann at Goddard described a new kind of gamma ray detector in this October 20, 1965, report. A spark chamber shows the path of a high-energy particle as a trail of sparks. Making that trail digital lets a computer record it directly. Gamma rays themselves leave no trail, but they can create particles that do, revealing their arrival.

Such detectors were built for satellites and high balloons. Gamma ray astronomy was a young field with few working instruments. A digitized chamber promised cleaner data with less hand work. Ehrmann presents the development for builders who would fly the next generation of instruments above the atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19660015109-the-electronics-brai:
H Doong and M Noordzy at Goddard described, in February 1966, the electronics unit that runs an X-ray telescope spectrometer in flight. They call it the electronics brain on board the experiment. Such an instrument must sequence its own work, handle its data, and answer commands from the ground. Its brain ties the telescope and spectrometer together as one system.

The catalog note says the paper covers system operation of that unit. A flaw in the logic could idle a costly experiment in orbit. Writing the operation down in full let the team test the design before flight. It also gave operators a shared picture of what the instrument would do on its own.
nasa-tm-19660021061-quasi-biennial-varia:
Kaichi Maeda at Goddard and T Suda of the Meteorological Research Institute in Tokyo studied a slow rhythm in cosmic ray counts, in this April 1966 paper. The rhythm repeats about every two years, which is what quasi-biennial means. Air temperature affects cosmic ray readings at the ground, Maeda notes at the start. A famous two-year oscillation in stratospheric winds offered a likely partner pattern.

Linking the two rhythms would tie deep space particles to Earth's own air. Ground cosmic ray records ran for decades, far longer than satellite data. If those records carry the stratosphere's rhythm, they gain a new use. The paper was prepared for a journal of geophysical research, where both fields could weigh the claim.
nasa-tm-19700025417-apollo-range-safety-:
The Mission Feasibility Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this working paper in January 1965. It sets the range safety destruct time delay for the Saturn 1B and Saturn 5 rockets. Range safety officers must be able to destroy a rocket that flies off course.

A time delay keeps the destruct system safe during the first moments of flight. The paper covers delays for flights that start with odd attitudes or uneven thrust. An addendum followed in August 1965. Rules of this kind protected the public near the launch site while the big rockets climbed away.
nasa-tm-19720005236-design-and-prelimina:
Thomas J Miller, James P Couch, and George M Prok of the Lewis Research Center designed this space radiator and reported first tests in November 1971, as NASA TM X-2401. A spacecraft can only shed waste heat by radiating it away. The radiator served an isotope Brayton power system with about seven kilowatts of electric output. It had to reject a much larger amount of heat. The design split that duty between two radiators in series.

Each radiator carried a backup coolant loop for safety. A single puncture or clog would not kill the power system. The report covers both the design and the early test results. Low temperature operation set this radiator apart from hotter designs. Such radiators were key hardware for long life space power.
nibelungenlied-shumway:
The Nibelungenlied, composed around 1200 by an unknown Austrian poet, is the great heroic epic of the German Middle Ages. Daniel Bussier Shumway's English translation is the text here. It tells of Siegfried the dragon-slayer and the fall of the Burgundian kings.

Siegfried wins the Nibelung treasure and the hand of Kriemhild, then helps King Gunther win the warrior queen Brunhild by stealth. A quarrel of queens ends in Siegfried's murder by the grim Hagen. Kriemhild's revenge, years later at the court of her new husband Etzel, drowns both courts in blood. The poem is Germany's national epic, as stark as any saga.
night-and-day: Virginia Woolf's 1919 novel, the most old-style of her books: two young London women weigh love against freedom, home against work. Katherine dreams of the stars while Mary fights for women's rights, and both must pick a path. Calm and finely drawn, it shows Woolf before she broke all the rules.
northumberland-yesterday-and-to-day:
Jean F. Terry published Northumberland Yesterday and To-day in 1913, inscribing it to Sir Francis Douglas Blake. Terry calls Blake an eminent Northumbrian, admired by the author. Chapters begin with the coast of Northumberland. North and South Tyne, then Down the Tyne, follow the rivers toward the sea.

Newcastle upon Tyne gets a chapter, and Elswick and its founder another. The Cheviots and the Roman Wall take the reader inland and back in time. Northumbrian streams, tales and legends, and ballads and poems close the contents. Pictures show Bamburgh Castle, Hexham Abbey, and the Roman Wall at Housesteads. Terry walks her home county with pride.
oliver-cromwell-a-play:
John Drinkwater wrote this stage play about Oliver Cromwell. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York. Drinkwater dedicated it to Bernard Shaw with homage. He calls Shaw the master dramatist of his age. The cast lists Cromwell's mother, wife, and daughter Bridget.

John Hampden and Henry Ireton appear as allies. Members of Parliament and the Speaker also enter. Seth and Amos Tanner give voices from below. The play treats Cromwell's rise and the Civil War era. Drinkwater writes history as intimate stage drama. It suits readers who like plays about power and faith.
oscar-or-the-boy-who-had-his-own-way:
Walter Aimwell wrote Oscar for his Aimwell Stories, a series of moral tales for boys published in Boston in the 1850s. In his preface he states the design plainly. Oscar is a bright but headstrong boy, over-indulged by his parents. He usually manages to have his own way by hook or by crook.

The story exhibits the bad consequences of a wayward and lawless spirit, and of sliding into indolent, untruthful, and disobedient habits. Other lessons of scarcely less importance are intermingled, the preface promises. Aimwell's method is the period's own: an attractive narrative of a boy's scrapes and winter scenes on Boston Common, engineered so that young readers absorb the warning while enjoying the tale.
podcast-joerogan-Gm8xFaM-raY:
Sam Harris returns for episode 641 of the Joe Rogan Experience, a middle entry in their long series of talks. Harris, the philosopher and neuroscientist, had by then published widely on religion, ethics, and the mind. His Rogan visits often become the show's most argued-over hours.

The two test their views on free will, moral truth, and how a person should live without faith in old doctrines. Harris keeps his cool, exact manner while Rogan answers from gut and practice. The episode shows their pairing in balance, before later years made Harris a more polarizing figure in Rogan's world.
podcast-joerogan-nWY_BXHZNAY:
Author Graham Hancock returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2051 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Hancock is the best known voice for the claim that a high culture fell in the Ice Age. His books and his TV series made the case to a vast crowd.

Hancock gives Rogan his latest form of the case, from new sites to new scans. He argues the proof grows each year while the experts look away. Rogan gives him the long form to lay it all out. Listeners get the claim whole from its top teller. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated case.
podcast-joerogan-v2oBLSDCZaY:
Thomas Campbell returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2541, a second long pass at his My Big TOE theory. Campbell, a physicist who worked on missile defense and NASA projects, argues reality is virtual. His model puts consciousness at the center of everything that exists.

Campbell restates the theory in fresh terms and answers the questions his first visit raised. He explains how a computing consciousness could render the world we touch. Rogan probes the testable parts and the spiritual ones. Open-minded listeners get a fuller map of a claim that physics and mysticism rarely share.
poems-by-the-way:
William Morris wrote the poems collected as Poems by the Way, first printed in 1891 and reprinted in a second edition by Longmans, Green in 1896. Morris, famous as a designer, craftsman, and socialist thinker, wrote verse all his life in a deliberately old-fashioned, story-loving style. The title means poems written along the way, beside his larger work, and the contents range widely.

Northern tales lead the list, with the wooing of Hallbiorn the Strong and Iceland First Seen reflecting Morris's love of the sagas. Love lyrics, battle pieces, and songs of labor follow, including the Message of the March Wind. The Voice of Toil, and the God of the Poor, where his politics enter the poetry openly. The book is a good single doorway into Morris the poet, minor works handled with major craft.
sevenoaks-a-story-of-today:
J. G. Holland published this novel of village life in 1875, here in a Grosset and Dunlap printing made with Scribner's. The town of Sevenoaks opens the tale, with Miss Butterworth at her evening pursuits. At town meeting, Mr. Belcher wins his point and the town's poor are auctioned off to keeper Thomas Buffum.

Jim Fenton arrives, takes lodgings at Buffum's boarding house, and finds an old friend. Soon the town stirs with commotion and fears that Benedict has met foul play. Holland mixes humor with a sharp look at how a small town treats its poor, its strangers, and its scandals.
shapes-of-clay:
Ambrose Bierce published this book of verse in 1903 and dedicated it to his young friends and pupils George Sterling and Herman Scheffauer. A preface owns that part of the book censures real persons by name, without their leave. Bierce offers no defense of his motives for writing or reprinting the pieces.

Many verses first ran in newspapers and return here much altered, drawn in part from his earlier Black Beetles in Amber. Satire, epitaph, and sharp portrait fill the pages. Bierce's acid wit, honed in California journalism, shapes clay men and women into brief, biting likenesses that spare few reputations.
shelley-an-essay:
An unnamed Catholic writer defends poetry's place in the Church in this essay on Shelley, printed by Burns and Oates in 1914. The essay mourns that the Church, once mother of poets and saints alike, has ceded song's glories to outsiders for two centuries. Dante and Dominic once grew in one soil, the writer notes.

Poetry, the essay holds, sinned and fell, and the Church cast her out instead of winning her back. That split harmed both faith and verse. Shelley stands as the test case: a rebel poet whom Catholic readers are urged to reclaim with love rather than fear.
sketches-by-boz-illustrative-of-every-da:
Charles Dickens published these sketches of London life under the pen name Boz, here in a 1903 Chapman and Hall printing with pictures by George Cruickshank and Phiz. A preface owns that Dickens wrote and issued the pieces one by one as a very young man. They form his first tries at authorship, he states.

Crude haste marks some pieces, Dickens grants, above all the tales. He left them near as first printed, since the public had received them kindly. Our Parish opens the set with beadle, parish engine, and schoolmaster. A great novelist's eye for street, shop, and clerk starts here.
stonehenge-today-yesterday:
Frank Stevens, curator of the Salisbury Museum, wrote Stonehenge: To-Day and Yesterday, printed at London in 1916 and priced at one shilling net. Heywood Sumner supplied the plans and illustrations, including a view of the stones as they probably once stood.

Stevens writes for visitors and general readers. They want to know what the great stone circle is. They want to know how it may have looked when complete. They want to know what state it stands in now. By setting the present ruins beside their likely past form, the book gives a short, plain guide to one of Britain's most famous ancient monuments and the questions that still surround it.
tales-of-hearsay:
Joseph Conrad's Tales of Hearsay gathers four late stories, with rights held from 1911, 1917, and 1918 by the Metropolitan Magazine Company. The contents list The Warrior's Soul, Prince Roman, The Tale, and The Black Mate.

The Warrior's Soul opens with an old officer scolding young men for judging his age group with too much ease. He recalls Napoleon's march into Russia, the long retreat, and the burning of Moscow. Readers meet Conrad's late style at work on war, pride, age, and pain, with each tale told at one remove, as if heard and passed on.
thackeray: G. K. Chesterton and Lewis Melville wrote Thackeray. James Pott and Company printed it in New York. Hodder and Stoughton printed it in London. Many plates fill the book. A portrait of William Makepeace Thackeray stands at the front. It comes from a drawing by Samuel Laurence. Headings promise three main parts. One treats the figures and places of Thackeray's books. One gives a note on his life. One gives notes on his portraits.
the-black-bearded-barbarian-the-life-of-:
Mary Esther Miller MacGregor, also known as Marion Keith, wrote a life of George Leslie Mackay. A footnote says the title was the name by which Mackay was known among the Chinese of north Formosa. Chapter one, called Splitting Rocks, starts behind a Canadian barn.

Boys have spent an afternoon breaking large stones for a new stone house their father is building. They pile brush on stones and let fire heat them until they crack, treating work as a picnic at first. By sunset, with meadowlarks gone to bed, they are tired and very hungry. One last fire, smelling of cedar, holds them before supper.
the-bridal-march-one-day:
Björnstjerne Björnson wrote The Bridal March and One Day, two tales translated from the Norwegian and put out in London by William Heinemann in 1896. A note on the books' past says The Bridal March was written in Christiania in 1872. The tale was composed as text to four designs by the Norwegian painter Tidemand, and was dedicated to Hans Christian Andersen.

The Bridal March itself opens in a high inland valley of Norway in the last century. There a fiddler has grown into a legend. Some of his tunes are said to come from the trolls, one from the devil himself, and one he made to save his life. The most famed of all is a bridal march, and its story, the tale says, does not end with his life.
the-broad-highway:
Jeffery Farnol wrote The Broad Highway, dated 1910. He dedicated it to Shirley Byron Jevons, the friend of his boyish ambitions. A note before the tale, the Ante Scriptum, tells how the book was born. On an early summer morning the author sat in the shade of a tree, eating fried bacon with a tinker. The thought came that he might write a book of his own.

That book would treat of roads and by-roads, of wind in lonely places, swift brooks and lazy streams. The tinker, told the plan aloud, objects: trees are only trees, and an inn an inn. More is needed. The author, a little damped, ticks items off on his fingers. There is a highwayman. There is Tom Cragg, the pugilist. There is a one-legged soldier of the Peninsula, an adventure at a lonely tavern, and a flight through woods at midnight.
the-child-s-day: Woods Hutchinson, A.M., M.D., a former state health officer of Oregon, wrote this health book for children in the Woods Hutchinson Health Series, copyrighted in 1912 by Houghton Mifflin. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The sections follow a child's day from waking, bathing, and breakfast through going to school, with lessons on fresh air, hearing, seeing, and drinking water.Its inside pages are not among what is present.
the-days-before-yesterday: Lord Frederick Hamilton opens The Days Before Yesterday with a foreword. The public welcome for an earlier book of his reminiscences, he explains, drew these memories from the lumber-room of recollection. He warns that readers hunting revelations or scandal will be disappointed: the book holds a record of events on different ground from the former volume. The contents range from his early days, Disraeli, and Sir Edwin Landseer to his first presentation to Queen Victoria and her letters. Only the foreword and part of the contents are present here.
the-epic-an-essay:
Lascelles Abercrombie's The Epic: An Essay, dated 1914, opens with a bold claim: epic poetry has been invented many times, in like states of society. Most nations, he says, pass through a heroic age, when their hot racial parts have not yet cooled into the calm routine of civic life. That heat makes the epic.

Abercrombie, who also wrote on Hardy and on prosody, tests his claim on Homer, Beowulf, and the great tales of the North and East. He asks what an epic is for, and whether a new age can bear one. The essay is short and deep.
the-extra-day: Algernon Blackwood is named on the title page of The Extra Day, printed at New York in 1915. His earlier books The Centaur and A Prisoner in Fairyland are listed below his name. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapter heads move from fact and fancy through wonder and time. They end with single chapters for Judy and for Tim. That hints at a tale built around how children meet wonder.
the-fair-maid-of-perth-or-st-valentine-s:
Sir Walter Scott set The Fair Maid of Perth, also called St. Valentine's Day, in old Perth, and the tale opens with a walk through Edinburgh's Canongate. The narrator boasts of the quarter's palace, abbey, and royal graves.

Scott lingers over Queen Mary's rooms and the solemn charm of a street steeped in past glory. That love of place and old story drives the novel, where a fair maid of Perth stands at the heart of feuds, crafts, and courtly danger. Guild pride, clan hate, and a king's weak rule shape the world she must move through.
the-foundations-an-extravagant-play: John Galsworthy wrote The Foundations as an extravagant play, one of his Fourth Series plays. Only the front matter and the first stage lines are present here. The cast names Lord William Dromondy, a member of Parliament, his wife, their staff, a poor family named Lemmy, and a crowd of sweated workers and anti-sweaters. The scenes move from a Park Lane wine cellar to a Bethnal Green room, all in one summer night after the Great War. No full act can be read here.
the-gilded-age-a-tale-of-today: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today. The title page is dated 1873. Only front matter is present here. It gives a contents list for Part 1, from Chapter I through Chapter IX. It also gives a long list of pictures. The chapter heads name Squire Hawkins and his Tennessee land. They name a move to Missouri, an adopted boy named Clay, and a steamboat blast. They also name Colonel Beriah Sellers, his grand schemes, and the death of Judge Hawkins.
the-king-s-highway: G. P. R. James wrote The King's Highway, a novel of the English Civil War era. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. None of the novel itself appears. The header gives the file as etext 3780, first posted in September 2001 and produced by Jim Tinsley in its tenth edition. Title and author are all that can be read. The highway itself stays out of reach. So do the cavaliers and roundheads who traveled it in James's pages.
the-life-and-death-of-richard-yea-and-na: Maurice Hewlett published his chronicle of Anjou in New York and London in 1901 and dedicated it to his friend Edmund Gosse. Only the title pages and the start of the contents are present here, naming book one as the Book of Yea and opening with an exordium by the Abbot Milo. Hewlett other works named on the page include The Forest Lovers and Little Novels of Italy. The tale of Richard and his noble lady is missing from this record.
the-life-of-the-spirit-and-the-life-of-t: Evelyn Underhill, author of Mysticism, published her study of spiritual life with Dutton in New York in 1922. Only the title page and contents are present here. Chapters cover the characters of spiritual life and history and the life of the spirit. Two further chapters join psychology to contemplation and suggestion. A preface is promised in the list as well. Underhill argument for a richer inner life in modern days cannot be seen in this record beyond those headings.
the-lighted-way: E. Phillips Oppenheim published his mystery novel in Boston in 1912, illustrated by A. B. Wenzell. Only the title page and contents are present here. Chapters cover an invitation to dinner, a face at the window, and an unusual errand. A gleam of steel and a cry that Rosario is dead follow in the list. Later titles promise a red signet ring and Sabatini doctrines. The thriller itself, by the author of Havoc and Peter Ruff, remains outside this record.
the-lyric-an-essay:
John Drinkwater's The Lyric, an essay dated 1922, asks what poetry is before it asks what a lyric is. Drinkwater begins with a comparison. Ask twenty intelligent people what the Thames is, he says, and each will answer, a river, yet that hardly satisfies an enquiring mind. Asking what they know of the Thames would bring geology, national history, praise of beauty, and personal confession instead.

The question "What is poetry?" has been answered innumerable times, he continues, often by the subtlest minds, and answered in as many ways. His contents promise a path through the best words in the best order, the degrees of poetry, Paradise Lost, a classification of poetry, and lyric forms such as song. Readers get a poet thinking aloud about his own art.
the-old-flute-player-a-romance-of-to-day: Edward Marshall and Charles T. Dazey wrote The Old Flute-Player, subtitled A Romance of To-day, published in New York in 1910, with illustrations by Clarence Rowe. Only the front matter and list of illustrations are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The picture captions hint at the plot: an Italian bully sprawls in the scuppers after Vanderlyn lifts an old man to his feet, and a voice cries, "She is not guilty! No; it is I."
the-old-santa-fe-trail-the-story-of-a-gr:
Colonel Henry Inman, a former assistant quartermaster in the United States Army, wrote the story of the Santa Fe Trail as a great highway. W. F. "Buffalo Bill" Cody supplied the preface. Cody praises Inman's account as truthful and thrilling, and recalls a West that once surpassed Russia or Africa in wild grandeur.

In the preface Cody describes the commerce of the prairies: slow freight caravans drawn by oxen and stage coaches pulled by mules crossing the plains. He credits the hardy pioneers, who fought the nomads of the desert, with making farms, states, and cities possible in the interior. Their hardships, he says, gave birth to the American homestead.
the-parts-men-play:
Arthur Beverley Baxter wrote The Parts Men Play, published in Toronto in 1920 and dedicated to his father, James Bennett Baxter. Lord Beaverbrook supplied the foreword. Beaverbrook calls Baxter his countryman and commends the book for its literary vitality and fresh outlook on Anglo-American feelings.

A Canadian, Beaverbrook argues, lives in a half-way house between Britain and the United States. He understands Britain by history, America by closeness, and Canada by birth. Baxter, formed by London journalism and English literature, is fitted to interpret the two sundered parts of the race to each other. The foreword promises essays of genial philosophy in that spirit.
the-picture-of-dorian-gray:
Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray appears here in the 1890 version of thirteen chapters. A short contents list gives the page span of each chapter before the story starts. Chapter I opens in a studio heavy with the smell of roses. Lilac and pink-flowering thorn scents drift in from the garden.

Lord Henry Wotton lies on a divan of Persian saddle-bags, smoking cigarettes. He watches the blossoms of a laburnum tree stir in the summer wind. Shadows of birds cross the silk curtains and put him in mind of Japanese painting. Bees murmur through the long grass outside, and the dim roar of London sounds beneath the stillness. The scene sets the talk-filled, beauty-loving world in which the portrait of the title will be painted.
the-round-up-a-romance-of-arizona-noveli:
John Murray and Marion Mills Miller novelized The Round-Up from Edmund Day's melodrama, calling it a romance of Arizona. The contents promise a cactus cross, a hold-up, a sky pilot, an atonement and a final chapter simply headed Jack.

Chapter one, The Cactus Cross, follows a mounted prospector down an old trail in the Ghost Range of northwestern Mexico, just across the Arizona border. His horse picks its way among broken granite blocks fallen from the mountain wall. Behind him a laden burro carries pack, bed-roll, pick, frying-pan and battered coffee-pot, stepping as sure-footedly as the mountain sheep that first formed the trail.
the-sorrows-of-a-show-girl-a-story-of-th: Kenneth McGaffey wrote these stories of Broadway chorus life in 1908, after they first appeared in the New York Morning Telegraph. Only the front matter and contents are present in this record. Fourteen chapters show Sabrina discoursing on theatrical conditions and receiving money and a fortune. She visits her parents in Emporia and shocks that staid town. She also attends the chorus girls' union ball and falls in love with a press agent, so her adventures themselves do not appear.
the-third-great-plague-a-discussion-of-s: John H. Stokes of the Mayo Clinic wrote The Third Great Plague, a discussion of syphilis for everyday people, published by W. B. Saunders in 1920 after first appearing in 1917. This record shows the title page and the first contents entries only. Those entries promise a history of syphilis, syphilis as a social problem, and the nature and course of the disease, including its prevalence. Stokes wrote to give lay readers straight medical facts, but his chapters themselves begin beyond the pages present here.
the-twenty-fourth-of-june-midsummer-s-da: Grace S. Richmond's Twenty-Fourth of June is subtitled Midsummer's Day and dated 1914. It is present here as title page and contents. Eighteen chapters open with the curtain rising on a home, then follow Richard as he changes his plans, pricks his fingers, and commits a traitorous proceeding. Later headings promise roses red, Mr. Kendrick entertaining, a chapter named 'The Taming of the Shrew,' lavender linen, and the nailing of a flag. Richmond's romance can be followed in outline, while her household speaks only beyond this record.
the-woman-s-way:
Charles Garvice's The Woman's Way was printed in 1914 by Hodder and Stoughton. Chapter one introduces Celia, climbing slowly to her room in Brown's Buildings. The stairs are steep, stony, and served by no lift. Whitewashed corridors make the place feel like a prison. Residents joke grimly and call it The Jail.

Celia has learned to climb slowly and save her strength. At twenty-two she is healthy and does not pause for breath. Only the milk boy and paper boy run those stairs. Garvice sets a working girl's hard lodging against her spirit. Readers can expect a popular romance grounded in shabby London rooms.
the-young-musician-or-fighting-his-way: Horatio Alger's The Young Musician, or Fighting His Way, appears here as a contents list of more than thirty chapters. Philip, the hero, starts as a candidate for the poorhouse. An auction, a fuss about a fiddle, and an escape follow. A reformed burglar and a professional engagement appear later. Rival musicians challenge Philip's rise. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
to-him-that-hath-a-tale-of-the-west-of-t: Ralph Connor called his book a novel of the West of today, and its contents list seventeen chapters. The Game opens the story, followed by the cost of sacrifice, a heathen quest, Annette, and the rectory. A grievance committee, a foreman, and free speech signal labour conflict ahead. Later headings bring a strike, gathering clouds, a storm, and a gallant fight, closing with Shall Be Given. A contents list alone is held in this record, so Connor's western novel itself does not appear.
toasts-and-forms-of-public-address-for-t: William Pittenger compiled toasts and forms of public address for speakers who wish to say the right thing in the right way. A contents list opens with after-dinner speeches ancient and modern, the value of a good story, and basic directions for speeches, toasts, and responses. Holiday speeches cover Independence Day, Memorial Day, Washington's Birthday, Christmas, and Thanksgiving. Presentation addresses, welcomes, wedding anniversaries, monument dedications, and political canvass speeches follow. A contents list alone is given in this record, so Pittenger's model speeches themselves are not shown.
tono-bungay:
H. G. Wells structured his novel in four books, and book one covers the days before Tono-Bungay was invented. Its first chapter treats Bladesover House, the narrator's mother, and the constitution of society. Most people, the narrator says, live in character, with congruous beginnings, middles, and ends.

Such people know their class, place, and proper tombstone size, like character actors playing a type. Another kind of life merely tastes life miscellaneously, jerked from its stratum by transverse force. Readers get a social novel that begins by questioning England's class order before its famous patent-medicine fortune appears.
two-little-women-on-a-holiday: Carolyn Wells's Two Little Women on a Holiday, made in the United States in 1917, is dedicated to her child friend Frances Althea Sprague. E. C. Caswell drew the frontispiece. The contents open with a wonderful plan and a favourable decision. Later chapters promise a merry quartette, a matinee idol, a skating party, and a lost jewel. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the holiday itself does not appear.
verses-and-rhymes-by-the-way: Nora Pembroke published Verses and Rhymes by the Way in Canada. A comic motto from Mansie Wauch fronts the book, with lines of Burns. She dedicated the book to Mrs. Irving, who drew near in Christian kindness in dark days. She promised never to forget the debt of love she owed. Pages present here hold front matter and the start of the contents only. Titles promise a story of Plantagenet and a legend of Buckingham Village. Poems on Ottawa, the Lake Allumette, and a mother's lament follow.
virginia-the-old-dominion-as-seen-from-i:
Frank and Cortelle Hutchins wrote Virginia: The Old Dominion as seen from its colonial waterway, the historic river James, in 1910. Their boat was the Gadabout, and the book, with a map and fifty-four plates from their own photographs, follows the river past ground made famous from Captain John Smith's day onward. A note explains that the volume first appeared as Houseboating on a Colonial Waterway, and was retitled for the See America First series.

They dedicated it to Francis E. Hutchins, father of one author and staunch friend of the Gadabout. The contents promise a first run to a cozy harbour, landfall at the country's birthplace, a run around Jamestown Island, fancies afloat and ruins ashore, and an old churchyard. Readers get a houseboat cruise through layers of history, where each turn of the river recalls a march of events and the figures who made them.
wallenstein-s-camp-a-play:
Frederich Schiller wrote The Camp of Wallenstein as an introduction to his tragedy of the same name. James Churchill made this English rendering. A note at the front explains the design. The camp piece paints the state of the general's army. That portrait gives the best clue to the spell of his huge power: blind faith in his unbroken success, and in the dark agencies said to secure it.

The soldiers live without restraint, the note says. They indulge every passion and hold no law but the camp's. The peasantry suffer hard oppression and plunder. A passage from Schiller's prologue adds that Wallenstein himself will not yet appear. His shadow stands in the bands his command alone could sway. Power, the prologue says, bore his heart astray, and his camp alone makes his crime clear. Churchill lets the marauders speak for themselves from there.
washington-s-birthday: Robert Haven Schauffler edited Washington's Birthday, a volume in the Our American Holidays series. Its subtitle promises the day's history, observance, spirit, and significance, told in prose and verse. A selection from Washington's own speeches and writings goes with it. Pages present here hold the title page, the editor's note of thanks to publishers who lent copyrighted pieces, and the start of the contents only. Early sections promise pieces by Oliver Wendell Holmes and Margaret E. Sangster. Charles W. Eliot, Hezekiah Butterworth, and Will Carleton follow.
what-the-animals-do-and-say:
Mrs. Follen wrote What the Animals Do and Say for young readers, with engraved pictures. The book opens as stories told by a mother, Mrs. Chilton, to her son Harry. Harry asks for a tale of strange people he has never heard of. His mother offers a people who travel each year of their lives.

These folk flee cold weather and meet in large family groups to plan the trip. They have no books, boats, or trains, yet never lose their way. Harry guesses they walk on four feet, and his mother laughs him off. The riddle points to wild birds and their flights. Tales of animal ways follow in talk form.
writing-the-photoplay: J. Berg Esenwein and Arthur Leeds wrote this manual on writing silent film plays. Leeds had edited scripts at the Edison Studio. Pages present here hold the title page and the start of a contents list for a revised edition, copyrighted in 1913 and 1919. Listed chapters ask what a photoplay is and who can write one. A chapter on photoplay terms follows. The teaching text itself does not appear in these pages.
